_note: The Story of Prophet Musa (Moses), drawn strictly from the Qur'an (Surahs Ta-Ha, al-Qasas, al-A'raf, ash-Shu'ara, Yunus, al-Baqarah, al-Kahf). Every event cites its ayat; verse text resolves from the loaded Qur'an reference. A couple of sound hadith (Sahih al-Bukhari) add context. No figural imagery; summaries carry no Arabic script.

places.name: The Junction of the Two Seas

events.title: Cast into the River
events.summary: As Pharaoh slaughters the sons of the Children of Israel, Allah inspires the mother of the newborn Musa to place him in the river, promising to return him to her and to make him one of the messengers. She sets the basket upon the water in trust.
events.why: The story opens with a mother's terror turned to trust: the very river Pharaoh uses to drown Israel's sons becomes the road that carries Musa safely into Pharaoh's own house.

events.title: Found by Pharaoh's Household
events.summary: Pharaoh's family draws the basket from the water. His wife pleads that the child be a comfort to them and not be killed, hoping he may benefit them or be taken as a son — not perceiving who he would become.
events.why: Allah places His prophet, unrecognised, in the household of the tyrant who feared him. The wife of Pharaoh, a believer, is the means of his safety.

events.title: Returned to His Mother
events.summary: The infant refuses every wet-nurse. His sister, following at a distance, offers to point them to a household that will nurse him — and so his own mother is brought to feed him. Allah returns him to her that her eye might be comforted and she know His promise is true.
events.why: The promise of 28:7 is kept at once: the child is restored to his mother, and Pharaoh unknowingly pays her to raise the very deliverer he dreaded.

events.title: The Man He Struck
events.summary: Grown, Musa enters the city and finds two men fighting — one of his people, one of Pharaoh's. He strikes the aggressor and the man dies. Musa grieves, saying this is from Satan's doing, and asks his Lord's forgiveness; and Allah forgives him.
events.why: Even a prophet's error becomes a moment of turning: Musa does not justify himself but seeks forgiveness, and the incident sets his flight from Egypt in motion.

events.title: Flight to Midian
events.summary: Warned that the chiefs are plotting to kill him, Musa leaves the city in fear and turns toward Midian, praying to be delivered from the wrongdoing people. Arriving at its water, he finds two women holding back their flock, waters it for them, and turns to the shade, asking his Lord for whatever good He might send.
events.why: Stripped of home and safety, Musa's first act in exile is service to strangers and reliance on Allah — the character of the man Allah is preparing to send back to Pharaoh.

events.title: Marriage and the Ten Years
events.summary: One of the two women returns shyly to invite him; her father, an honourable elder, hears his story and reassures him. Judging Musa strong and trustworthy, he offers him a daughter in marriage in return for hiring himself for eight years, or ten if he wishes. Musa agrees.
events.why: Years of quiet, honest labour in Midian temper the fugitive into a shepherd and a husband — the training Allah gives His prophet before the mountain and the mission.

events.title: The Fire at the Mountain
events.summary: Travelling by night, Musa sees a fire by the mount and goes for a brand to guide his family. There he is called: 'I am Allah; there is no god but Me, so worship Me and establish prayer.' His staff becomes a serpent, his hand comes out shining white — two signs — and he is commanded to go to Pharaoh, who has transgressed.
events.why: This is the hinge of the whole story: the shepherd of Midian is made Kalim Allah, the one Allah speaks to, and is sent back to the land he fled — armed only with the truth and two signs.

events.title: Harun Given as a Helper
events.summary: Musa prays for his breast to be expanded, his task made easy, and a knot loosed from his tongue, and asks that his brother Harun be appointed as a helper and share his mission. Allah grants his whole request.
events.why: The prophet does not go alone or in his own strength: he asks for ease, for clear speech, and for his brother — and Allah answers every part, joining Harun to him as a prophet.

events.title: Before Pharaoh
events.summary: Musa and Harun come to Pharaoh: 'We are messengers of the Lord of the worlds — send the Children of Israel with us.' Pharaoh mocks him, recalls the man he killed, and demands, 'And what is the Lord of the worlds?' Musa answers: the Lord of the heavens and the earth and all between them.
events.why: The confrontation is set as a contest between two claims of lordship — Pharaoh's over Egypt and Allah's over all creation — and Musa answers tyranny not with fear but with the plain truth of tawhid.
events.locator2: Book of the Prophets, no. 3340 — the intercession: Mūsā, the one to whom Allah spoke

events.title: The Duel with the Magicians
events.summary: On a day of festival Pharaoh gathers his finest magicians. They cast their ropes and staffs, which seem to slither by their spell; Musa is told not to fear. He casts his staff and it swallows all their falsehood. The magicians fall down in prostration, declaring belief in the Lord of Musa and Harun — and defy Pharaoh's threats.
events.why: The very experts Pharaoh summoned to defeat Musa are the first to believe: they know real signs from trickery, and choose faith over Pharaoh's crucifixion — the truth's first public victory.

events.title: The Signs upon Egypt
events.summary: Pharaoh's people are seized with years of drought and shortage of fruits, that they might take heed. When they still turn away, Allah sends upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood — clear signs, one after another — yet they remain arrogant, a criminal people.
events.why: Sign after sign is sent as mercy and warning, so none can say they were not shown the truth; Pharaoh's persistence is a choice, made against overwhelming proof.

events.title: The Command to Depart
events.summary: Allah reveals to Musa to travel by night with His servants, for they will be pursued. Pharaoh sends into the cities to muster his forces against the small band who have angered him — and so the Children of Israel set out toward the sea with Pharaoh's army at their backs.
events.why: The deliverance from Egypt begins in secrecy and danger: a slave people, leaving in the night, hemmed between the sea before them and Pharaoh's chariots behind.

events.title: The Parting of the Sea
events.summary: At the sea's edge Musa's people fear they are overtaken; he answers, 'No! Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me.' Commanded to strike the sea with his staff, it parts into towering walls with a dry path between. The Children of Israel cross; Pharaoh and his army follow into the parted way — and the sea returns upon them.
events.why: The climax of the exodus: the same sea that opens as a road of rescue for the believers closes as a grave for the tyrant. Faith's certainty — 'my Lord is with me' — is vindicated before all.
events.locator2: Book of Fasting, no. 2004 — the fast of ʿĀshūrāʾ commemorating Mūsā's deliverance

events.title: The Drowning of Pharaoh
events.summary: As the water overtakes him, Pharaoh cries out that he believes there is no god but the One the Children of Israel believe in. The answer comes: 'Now? — when before you disobeyed and were of the corrupters?' Yet his body is preserved as a sign to those who come after.
events.why: Faith declared only when escape is gone is no faith at all. Pharaoh's drowning, and the preserving of his body, stand as a lasting warning against pride that repents too late.

events.title: Manna and the Quails
events.summary: In the wilderness Allah shades the Children of Israel with clouds and sends down upon them the manna and the quails: 'Eat from the good things We have provided you.' They wronged not Allah, but were wronging themselves by their ingratitude.
events.why: Freed from Egypt, the people are carried by pure provision — food and shade from the sky — a mercy meant to teach gratitude, which they so often forgot.

events.title: The Appointment at Mount Sinai
events.summary: Musa is appointed thirty nights, completed with ten, to meet his Lord — forty nights — leaving Harun over the people. He asks, 'My Lord, show me, that I may look at You.' He is told he will not see Him; the mountain, when its Lord appears to it, is crushed level, and Musa falls unconscious. He is given the Tablets — guidance and detail for all things.
events.why: At the mountain the Law is given and the limits of even a prophet's sight are shown: Musa cannot behold Allah in this life, yet receives His guidance in the Tablets to carry to his people.

events.title: The Golden Calf
events.summary: In Musa's absence, as-Samiri fashions from their ornaments a calf — a mere body that lows — and many of the people take it as a god, though Harun warns them and calls them back. Musa returns angry and grieved, casts down the Tablets, takes his brother's head, then hears Harun's plea and turns to confront as-Samiri.
events.why: The greatest danger to the people is not Pharaoh's army but their own hearts: within weeks of the sea they turn to a calf. Harun's restraint and Musa's zeal together guard tawhid against the idol.

events.title: Musa and al-Khidr
events.locator2: Book of Knowledge, no. 74 — Mūsā seeks al-Khiḍr
events.summary: Seeking a servant of Allah given special knowledge, Musa meets al-Khidr at the junction of the two seas and asks to follow and learn. Al-Khidr warns he will not be able to bear patience. He scuttles a boat, takes the life of a boy, and rebuilds a falling wall without pay — each time Musa objects — then explains: the boat was spared from a seizing king, the boy would have burdened his believing parents, and the wall guarded an orphans' treasure. Then they part.
events.why: Even Kalim Allah is sent to learn: that Allah's wisdom often lies hidden beneath events that seem wrong to us, and that patience with what we cannot yet understand is itself a kind of knowledge.

events.title: The Shyness of Mūsā, and the Fleeing Stone
events.locator: Book of the Prophets, no. 3404 — Allah clears Mūsā of what the Children of Israel alleged
events.locator2: Surah al-Aḥzāb 33:69 — 'Be not like those who abused Mūsā; then Allah cleared him of what they said'
events.summary: Mūsā was so modest that he kept his body fully covered, and some of the Children of Israel slandered him, claiming he hid a bodily defect. Allah willed to clear him: as Mūsā bathed alone, laying his clothes on a stone, the stone fled with them, and he ran after it calling, 'My garment, O stone!' — until he reached a group of the Children of Israel, who saw him and found him the best of what Allah had created, free of any defect. This, the Prophet ﷺ said, is Allah's clearing of him in the verse of al-Aḥzāb.
events.why: The Qur'an commands the believers not to be like those who abused Mūsā, 'then Allah cleared him.' This ḥadīth narrates the very incident the verse points to — how Allah defends His prophets' honour.

events.title: Mūsā and the Angel of Death
events.locator: Book of the Prophets, no. 3407 — the Angel of Death is sent to Mūsā, and Mūsā asks to die near the Holy Land
events.summary: When the Angel of Death came to Mūsā, Mūsā slapped him on the eye. The angel returned to his Lord saying, 'You sent me to a servant who does not want to die.' Allah told him to return and tell Mūsā to place his hand on the back of an ox — for every hair it covered, a year of life. Mūsā asked what would come after that; told 'then death,' he asked to die then, and begged to be brought within a stone's throw of the Holy Land. The Prophet ﷺ said that were he there, he would show them Mūsā's grave beside the road, by the red sand-hill.
events.why: Even the prophet who spoke with Allah met death, and chose nearness to the Holy Land at its coming — a sign of how the messengers loved that blessed ground.

events.title: Holding Fast to the Throne
events.locator: Book of the Prophets, no. 3398 — Mūsā found holding a pillar of the Throne on the Day of Resurrection
events.summary: The Prophet ﷺ said: on the Day of Resurrection the people will be struck unconscious, and he will be the first to recover — and he will find Mūsā already holding fast to one of the pillars of the Throne of Allah, not knowing whether Mūsā recovered before him, or was among those Allah exempted from the swoon, for the unconsciousness Mūsā had already been given at the Mount (Ṭūr).
events.why: The prophet who fell senseless when his Lord appeared to the mountain is, at the end, found nearest the Throne — the honour of the one Allah spoke to directly.

paths.title: The Arc of Musa
paths.blurb: Seven turning points from a basket on the river, through Midian and the fire at the mountain, to the parting of the sea and the Law at Sinai.

paths.title: The Confrontation with Pharaoh
paths.blurb: From the first audience in the court to the duel with the magicians and the parting of the sea — truth against tyranny.

paths.title: The Law and the Wilderness
paths.blurb: After the sea: provision in the desert, the Tablets at Sinai, the golden calf, and the lessons of al-Khidr.
